citations.quote: Let $I$ be a nonempty finite or countably infinite set equipped with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies, let $g_i>0$ be weights, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open parameter interval. For a nonnegative family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ define $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup_{F\subset I,\,F\text{ finite}}\sum_{i\in F}a_i$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the supremum as in [[def-complete-ordered-field]] when the finite subsums are bounded; set the value to $+\infty$ when they are unbounded. This definition is independent of the specified enumeration. For $\beta\in J$, define the nonnegative partition sum $Z(\beta):=\sum_{i\in I}g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ by this rule. The admissible parameter set is $J_Z:=\{\beta\in J:0<Z(\beta)<\infty\}$. For $\beta\in J_Z$, define $p_i(\beta):=g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)/Z(\beta)$; then $(p_i)$ is a countable probability law. For any real observable $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

Let $I,E_i,g_i,J,Z$ be as in [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]. Suppose that for every compact interval $K\subset J$ there is a summable sequence $a_i\ge0$ such that $g_i(1+|E_i|^2)\exp(-\beta E_i)\le a_i$ for every $i\in I$ and $\beta\in K$. Then $Z$ is positive, finite, and $C^2$ on $J$, with $Z'(\beta)=-\sum_i g_iE_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ and $Z''(\beta)=\sum_i g_iE_i^2\exp(-\beta E_i)$. The probabilities $p_i$ are normalized; their mean $\bar E$ and variance are finite and satisfy $-\partial_\beta\log Z=\bar E$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$. Moreover $H_g(p)=\log Z+\beta\bar E$, and its defining series is absolutely convergent.

derivations.claim: Direct summation gives $Z=1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon}=1+q$, hence $p_1=q/(1+q)$ and $p_0=1/(1+q)$.

The finite weighted sum gives $\bar E=\varepsilon p_1=\varepsilon q/(1+q)$. The second centered moment is $p_0(0-\bar E)^2+p_1(\varepsilon-\bar E)^2=\varepsilon^2q/(1+q)^2$, which is positive because $q\in(0,1)$. The values also agree with the finite-list derivative identities of [F2].

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

The **expectation** of a real random variable $X$ on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is
$$\mathbb E[X]:=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega).$$
For a real constant $c$, the notation $c$ also denotes the constant random variable $\omega\mapsto c$.

For real random variables $X$ and $Y$ on one finite probability space, define
$$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2],\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$
The **standard deviation** of $X$ is $\sigma_X:=\operatorname{Var}(X)^{1/2}$, using the unique nonnegative square root supplied by [[thm-of-square-roots]]. Variance is nonnegative because its defining random variable is pointwise nonnegative and expectation is a sum with nonnegative weights.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

derivations.claim: Let $S_N=\sum_{n=0}^Nq^n$. Multiplying this finite sum by $1-q$ gives $(1-q)S_N=1-q^{N+1}$. Since $q=e^{-\gamma}$ for $\gamma>0$, [F5] gives $q^{N+1}\to0$; hence $Z=(1-q)^{-1}$ and the weights $(1-q)q^n$ sum to one. On a compact $\gamma$-interval $[b,B]\subset(0,\infty)$, set $a_n=(1+n^2)e^{-bn}$. Then $a_{n+1}/a_n=e^{-b}(1+(n+1)^2)/(1+n^2)\to e^{-b}<1$. Choose $c$ with $e^{-b}<c<1$; for all sufficiently large $n$, $a_{n+1}\le ca_n$, so the tail is bounded by a convergent geometric series. Thus $\sum_n(1+n^2)e^{-\gamma n}\le\sum_na_n<\infty$, which is the local envelope required by [F1].

With $Z(\gamma)=(1-e^{-\gamma})^{-1}$, [F1] gives $\mathbb E n=-\partial_\gamma\log Z=q/(1-q)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(n)=\partial_\gamma^2\log Z=q/(1-q)^2$. Substitution $q=e^{-\gamma}$ and [F4] justify the parameter derivatives. Therefore $\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(n)}/\mathbb E n=1/\sqrt q\to1$ as $q\uparrow1$.

The fermionic partition sum is $1+q$; its two probabilities are $1/(1+q)$ and $q/(1+q)$. Their finite weighted sums give mean $q/(1+q)$ and variance $q/(1+q)^2$, equal to the mean times one minus the mean.
These are calculations for the two specified probability laws only; no independence, physical preparation, or measured fluctuation claim is used.

citations.quote: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where the Borel sets of the extended real line are the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, writing $d = n + 1 - m$
for the number of terms,

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and $S \subseteq F$.

- $u \in F$ is an **upper bound** of $S$ if $s \le u$ for all $s \in S$; $S$ is
  **bounded above** if it has an upper bound.
- $u \in F$ is a **least upper bound** (or **supremum**, $\sup S$) of $S$ if $u$
  is an upper bound of $S$ and $u \le u'$ for every upper bound $u'$ of $S$.

$F$ is a **complete ordered field** (equivalently, $F$ has the
**least-upper-bound property**, or is **Dedekind complete**) if every nonempty
$S \subseteq F$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $F$.

derivations.claim: The simple minorants of $f_n$ are also minorants of $f_{n+1}$, so their integral suprema increase. Each is at most $\int f$; hence $L:=\lim_n\int f_n$ exists in $[0,\infty]$ and $L\le\int f$.

Fix a nonnegative simple $s\le f$ and $0<t<1$. The measurable sets $A_n:=\{f_n\ge ts\}$ increase and cover $\{s>0\}$, since $f_n(x)\to f(x)\ge s(x)>ts(x)$ there. Write $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{B_j}$ in disjoint level form. For each $c_j>0$, $A_n\cap B_j\uparrow B_j$; countable additivity, applied to successive disjoint differences, gives $\mu(A_n\cap B_j)\uparrow\mu(B_j)$. The finite-sum definition [F2] then gives $\int s\mathbf1_{A_n}\uparrow\int s$. As $f_n\ge ts\mathbf1_{A_n}$, monotonicity and homogeneity of the simple integral imply $L\ge t\int s$. Let $t\uparrow1$ and take the supremum over $s\le f$; [F1, F3] give $L\ge\int f$. Together with step 1.1 this proves monotone convergence.

For nonnegative measurable $f$, define $s_n:=2^{-n}\sum_{k=1}^{n2^n}\mathbf1_{\{f\ge k2^{-n}\}}$. Each $s_n$ is a finite-valued measurable simple function. Every threshold counted in $s_n$ is also counted at the even-index threshold in $s_{n+1}$, so $s_n\le s_{n+1}$. If $f(x)<\infty$, once $n>f(x)$ the mesh gives $0\le f(x)-s_n(x)<2^{-n}$; if $f(x)=\infty$, then $s_n(x)=n$. Thus $s_n\uparrow f$. Define $t_n:=2^{-n}\sum_{k=1}^{n2^n}\mathbf1_{\{g\ge k2^{-n}\}}$; the same threshold and mesh argument shows $t_n\uparrow g$. Apply step 1.1 to $s_n$, $t_n$, and $s_n+t_n$. Refine their finitely many level sets to the finite partition of intersections $B_j\cap C_k$; regrouping the resulting sums by [F2] gives $\int(s_n+t_n)=\int s_n+\int t_n$. Passing to the three monotone limits proves $\int(f+g)=\int f+\int g$.

For $c>0$, simple minorants of $cf$ are exactly $c$ times simple minorants of $f$, so the supremum definition gives $\int cf=c\int f$; for $c=0$ both sides are zero. If an integrable real function is expressed as $u-v$ with $u,v\ge0$ integrable, the value $\int u-\int v$ is independent of the expression: $u-v=u'-v'$ implies $u+v'=u'+v$, and step 2.2 equates the finite sums of integrals. The definition using positive and negative parts is one such expression, so signed integrals are linear.

For f=0, the explicit approximants in step 2.2 are identically zero.
For f=1 on a finite measure space, step 2.2 approximates it from below by simple thresholds.

Step 2.1 lets t increase to 1 after proving the bound for every 0<t<1.
Steps 2.1 and 2.2 choose no sequence of witnesses; the approximants are explicitly defined.

citations.quote: Let $I$ be a nonempty finite or countably infinite set equipped with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies, let $g_i>0$ be weights, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open parameter interval. For a nonnegative family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ define $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup_{F\subset I,\,F\text{ finite}}\sum_{i\in F}a_i$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the supremum as in [[def-complete-ordered-field]] when the finite subsums are bounded; set the value to $+\infty$ when they are unbounded. This definition is independent of the specified enumeration. For $\beta\in J$, define the nonnegative partition sum $Z(\beta):=\sum_{i\in I}g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ by this rule. The admissible parameter set is $J_Z:=\{\beta\in J:0<Z(\beta)<\infty\}$. For $\beta\in J_Z$, define $p_i(\beta):=g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)/Z(\beta)$; then $(p_i)$ is a countable probability law. For any real observable $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,

derivations.claim: Factor $e^{-\beta E_0}$ from the partition sum to obtain $Z=e^{-\beta E_0}(g+\sum_{i:E_i>E_0}e^{-\beta(E_i-E_0)})$. citations.quote: For every fixed $\beta>0$, the sequence $p_L(\beta)$ of [[def-tdmath-bounded-finite-range-lattice]] has a finite limit as $L\to\infty$. If another finite-volume energy $\widetilde H_L$ on the same configurations satisfies $\sup_s|\widetilde H_L(s)-H_L(s)|\le C_bL^{d-1}$ for a constant $C_b$ independent of $L$, define $\widetilde Z_L(\beta):=\sum_{s\in\mathcal A^{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta\widetilde H_L(s)}$ and $\widetilde p_L(\beta):=L^{-d}\log\widetilde Z_L(\beta)$. Then $\widetilde p_L$ has the same limit. The result covers finite-alphabet, bounded, translation-invariant finite-range interactions on cubic boxes; it asserts no continuum-particle or long-range limit.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

The **expectation** of a real random variable $X$ on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is
$$\mathbb E[X]:=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega).$$
For a real constant $c$, the notation $c$ also denotes the constant random variable $\omega\mapsto c$.

For real random variables $X$ and $Y$ on one finite probability space, define
$$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2],\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$
The **standard deviation** of $X$ is $\sigma_X:=\operatorname{Var}(X)^{1/2}$, using the unique nonnegative square root supplied by [[thm-of-square-roots]]. Variance is nonnegative because its defining random variable is pointwise nonnegative and expectation is a sum with nonnegative weights.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Differentiating the finite sum gives $p_L'=-L^{-d}\mathbb E_{\beta,L}H_L$ and $p_L''=L^{-d}\operatorname{Var}_{\beta,L}(H_L)\ge0$. Thus $p_L$ is convex. Passing the two-point convexity inequality to the pointwise limit shows that $p$ is convex too.

For any small $h>0$ with $\beta\pm h\in J$, convexity and differentiability of $p_L$ give $[p_L(\beta)-p_L(\beta-h)]/h\le p_L'(\beta)\le[p_L(\beta+h)-p_L(\beta)]/h$. Take lower and upper limits in $L$, use [F1], then let $h\downarrow0$; differentiability of $p$ forces $p_L'(\beta)\to p'(\beta)$. The identity in step 1.1 yields the claimed mean limit.

Fix $t>0$ small enough that $\beta\pm t\in J$. For the upper tail, the pointwise inequality $\mathbf1_{\{H_L\ge L^d(e+\varepsilon)\}}\le e^{t(H_L-L^d(e+\varepsilon))}$ and finite summation give $\mathbb P(H_L/L^d\ge e+\varepsilon)\le\exp\{L^d[p_L(\beta-t)-p_L(\beta)-t(e+\varepsilon)]\}$. Differentiability of $p$ and $e=-p'(\beta)$ imply $p(\beta-t)=p(\beta)+te+o(t)$; choose $t$ so the bracket's limit is at most $-3t\varepsilon/4$. Pointwise convergence at $\beta-t$ and $\beta$ then makes the bracket at most $-t\varepsilon/2$ for all sufficiently large $L$.

For the lower tail use $\mathbf1_{\{H_L\le L^d(e-\varepsilon)\}}\le e^{-t(H_L-L^d(e-\varepsilon))}$; its expectation is $\exp\{L^d[p_L(\beta+t)-p_L(\beta)+t(e-\varepsilon)]\}$. Since $p(\beta+t)=p(\beta)-te+o(t)$, possibly reducing $t$ and increasing $L_0$ makes this at most $e^{-L^dt\varepsilon/2}$. Adding both tail bounds yields the result with $c=t\varepsilon/2$.

Steps 1.2–2.2 bound the two tails whose union is $\{|H_L/L^d-e|\ge\varepsilon\}$; the theorem is conditional on differentiability of $p$ and does not assert convergence of second derivatives or equivalence for arbitrary observables.

For any real observable $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

Let $\alpha,\beta$ be two one-component phase branches from [[def-td-phase-and-coexistence-domain]] on a common open chart $O\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ with coordinates $(T,p)$. Assume each branch has a local $C^2$ energy representation $\mathcal U_i(s,V,n)$, $i\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$, and that within each fixed branch tag it satisfies the same-tag homogeneity
$$
\mathcal U_i(\lambda s,\lambda V,\lambda n)=\lambda\mathcal U_i(s,V,n)
$$
for all $\lambda$ in a neighborhood of $1$ for which the scaled state remains in the chart. This is a phase-branch hypothesis: the general tagged law of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]] does not imply it. It may be stipulated independently on each local branch, or supplied by the common-law bulk subclass of [[pthm-td-euler-and-gibbs-duhem]] when each phase's local inverse states lie in its designated entropy cone with fixed species and intensive parameters and common SI units and energy/entropy reference conventions. That supplied subclass uses local inverse uniqueness and does not require a global energy inverse.

Suppose a state $(T_0,p_0)\in O$ is an attained interior coexistence equilibrium with bilateral energy, volume, and species exchange between the two branches, and both branches admit the valid local Gibbs charts of [[def-td-legendre-potentials]]. Write $g_i=G_i/n_i$, $s_i=S_i/n_i$, and $v_i=V_i/n_i$ in the units specified by [[def-td-si-quantities]]. If
$$
\Delta v(T_0,p_0):=v_\beta(T_0,p_0)-v_\alpha(T_0,p_0)\ne0,
$$
then, on some open interval about $T_0$, the equal-Gibbs-per-mole coexistence condition $g_\alpha(T,p(T))=g_\beta(T,p(T))$ defines a unique local $C^1$ curve and
$$
\frac{dp}{dT}=\frac{s_\beta-s_\alpha}{v_\beta-v_\alpha}.
$$
If, in addition, conversion from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ is admitted as a reversible process in contact with an ideal thermal reservoir at the same fixed $T$, then its molar latent heat absorbed by the system is $\ell_{\alpha\to\beta}=T(s_\beta-s_\alpha)$. These are conditional model deductions. The slope conclusion is not asserted when $\Delta v=0$ or where the branch charts are not $C^1$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

derivations.claim:
At $(T_0,p_0)$, differentiation gives $S_i/n_i=s_i$, $V_i/n_i=v_0$, and $\mu_i=g_i=g_0$. Also $U_{i,T}=n_i c$, $V_{i,p}=-n_i\kappa$, and $V_{i,T}=0$, so the derivative determinant for $(T,p)\mapsto(U_i,V_i)$ at fixed positive amount is $-n_i^2c\kappa\ne0$. Thus [L1] supplies valid local state charts. The branch equality function is
$$
F(T,p):=g_\beta-g_\alpha=-(s_\beta-s_\alpha)(T-T_0),
$$
whose zero set is $T=T_0$ with every nearby chart pressure permitted.

Here $\Delta v=v_\beta-v_\alpha=0$, so the zero set is not the graph of a unique pressure as a function of temperature on an open interval about $T_0$, and the quotient $\Delta s/\Delta v$ is undefined. The nonzero-jump hypothesis of [F1] fails, so this model does not contradict that theorem.

Let $d\ge1$, and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty compact set of dimensionless phase-generator coordinates. A generator point $x\in K$ encodes one model-specified homogeneous phase state, with declared entropy per mole $s(x)$ in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$; let $s:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Define $\operatorname{conv}K$ as the set of finite convex combinations of points of $K$, and fix $\bar x\in\operatorname{conv}K$. Use the Borel sigma algebra relative to $K$, and let $\delta_x$ denote unit point mass at $x$. The vector integral $\int_Kx\,dP$ is taken coordinatewise. Assume every Borel probability mixture $P$ on $K$ with $\int_Kx\,dP(x)=\bar x$ is feasible and has entropy per mole $\int_Ks(x)\,dP(x)$. Then the entropy maximum over all such mixtures is attained by a finite atomic mixture with at most $d+1$ phase-generator states.

Here the integral uses the measure convention of [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]]. The entropy map includes its physical entropy units and is part of the model; this theorem does not derive the microscopic meaning of entropy or assert that a physical phase domain is compact.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where the Borel sets of the extended real line are the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

derivations.claim:
Since $0< s_0-a\le s(x)\le s_0$, every feasible $s$ is nonnegative and bounded. For $n\ge2$, put $A_n:=\{x\in K:|x|\ge1/n\}$. Their union is $K$; since $P(K)=1$, countable additivity implies $P(A_n)>0$ for some $n$. On $A_n$, $s\le s_0-a/n$, and on its complement $s\le s_0$. For any nonnegative simple function $\varphi\le s$, the measure integral definition [F2] therefore gives
$$
\int_K\varphi\,dP\le (s_0-a/n)P(A_n)+s_0P(K\setminus A_n)=s_0-aP(A_n)/n<s_0.
$$
Indeed, refine the finitely many level sets of $\varphi$ by $A_n$ and its complement; each simple-function coefficient is bounded by the corresponding pointwise bound on that piece, so the simple-integral formula [F2] gives the inequality. The common strict upper bound is independent of $\varphi$, hence its supremum also satisfies $\int_Ks\,dP<s_0$.

For each $0<\epsilon<1$, the measure $P_\epsilon=\tfrac12\delta_{-\epsilon}+\tfrac12\delta_{\epsilon}$ is supported on $K$, has mean zero, and satisfies $\int s\,dP_\epsilon=s_0-a\epsilon$. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ shows that the supremum is $s_0$. Step 1.1 shows that no feasible measure attains it. This lies outside the compactness hypothesis in [F1] and exhibits a finite supremum without a maximizing mixture.

Take $\Omega$ to be a finite nonempty microstate set as in [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]: distinct elements count as distinct microstates, and the physical energy values are finite and measured in joules in the declared rest frame. Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and stage energy functions $E_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$ for $k=0,\ldots,m$, with the energy offsets fixed by the declared protocol model. Fix inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$. The finite partition sum and canonical probability vector at stage $k$ are $Z_k=\sum_{i\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E_k(i)}$ and $\pi_k(i)=e^{-\beta E_k(i)}/Z_k$. Since $\Omega$ is nonempty and finite and each energy is finite, $0<Z_k<\infty$ and $\pi_k$ is a strictly positive probability vector.

A transition kernel at stage $k$ is a matrix $K_k(i,j)\ge0$ with $\sum_{j\in\Omega}K_k(i,j)=1$. In the forward stage order, the energy changes instantaneously from $E_{k-1}$ to $E_k$ while the state is still $i_{k-1}$; the subsequent bath transition samples $i_k$ using $K_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$ at fixed energy $E_k$. A path is $\omega=(i_0,\ldots,i_m)\in\Omega^{m+1}$. For an initial law $\mu_0$, its path probability is $P_F(\omega)=\mu_0(i_0)\prod_{k=1}^mK_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$.

Work on the system is positive when energy is supplied to it, and heat into the system is positive when a bath transition raises its energy. Define $W(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_{k-1})-E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})]$ and $Q_{\mathrm{in}}(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_k)-E_k(i_{k-1})]$, both in joules. Define $F_k=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_k$ and $\Delta F=F_m-F_0=-\beta^{-1}\log(Z_m/Z_0)$. These are finite-model quantities; their physical interpretation is conditional on the adopted preparation and transition assumptions.

A finite rate model consists of a finite nonempty state set $S$ and rates $q_{ij}\ge0$ in seconds$^{-1}$ for $i
e j$. Set $q_{ii}=-\sum_{j
e i}q_{ij}$. A row probability vector is $p=(p_i)_{i\in S}$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$. Its time-dependent law $p(t)$ follows the continuous-time master equation $\dot p_i=\sum_{j
e i}[p_jq_{ji}-p_iq_{ij}]$. A strictly positive normalized vector $\pi$ is a detailed-balance law when $\pi_iq_{ij}=\pi_jq_{ji}$ for every distinct pair. Its undirected rate graph has an edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $\pi_iq_{ij}>0$; detailed balance makes this equivalent to $\pi_jq_{ji}>0$.

For a discrete transition kernel $K$ on a finite state set, $\pi$-detailed balance means $\pi_iK(i,j)=\pi_jK(j,i)$ for every pair. If $\pi$ is strictly positive, this identity pairs the supports of forward and reversed transitions. A rate model or a reversible kernel is a mathematical/physical model class; no observed trajectory is asserted by the definition.

For a protocol of [[def-td-driven-finite-path-model]], fix a bath temperature $T_b>0$ kelvin and set $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T_b)^{-1}$ in joules$^{-1}$, using the exact constant and SI conventions of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. The finite-state clause of the adopted [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] then gives the stage-zero law $\pi_0(i)=e^{-\beta E_0(i)}/Z_0$; adopt that the initial microstate is drawn from this law, so $\mu_0=\pi_0$. Here $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty and $E_0(i)$ is finite, so $0<Z_0<\infty$ as required by that clause. This is a model premise about the preparation distribution. It does not follow from the finite partition-sum definition, does not assert that an arbitrary system equilibrates in finite time, and does not report a measured preparation. The countable-state and measure-integral branches of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] are not used.

For the protocol in [[def-td-driven-finite-path-model]], adopt, at each stage $k=1,\ldots,m$, the stationarity condition $\sum_{i\in\Omega}\pi_k(i)K_k(i,j)=\pi_k(j)$ for every $j\in\Omega$. This says that if the bath transition begins with law $\pi_k$ at fixed energy $E_k$, it ends with the same law. It is a physical modeling assumption for this protocol family, not a consequence of the transition-kernel definition and not an assertion that the kernel mixes every initial law to $\pi_k$.
For every path $\omega=(i_0,\ldots,i_m)$ of [[def-td-driven-finite-path-model]], the endpoint energy change is $E_m(i_m)-E_0(i_0)=W(\omega)+Q_{\mathrm{in}}(\omega)$, with the stated sign convention.

derivations.claim: Define the reverse path law by starting with $\pi_m(i_m)$ and, in reverse order, using $K_k(i_k,i_{k-1})$ at fixed energy $E_k$ before undoing that quench. By detailed balance, if $K_k(i_{k-1},i_k)>0$ then $K_k(i_k,i_{k-1})>0$, because $\pi_k$ is strictly positive. Thus positive forward paths pair with positive reverse paths.

On a paired path, divide the endpoint Gibbs weights and use detailed balance for each transition: $P_F(\omega)/P_R(\omega^R)=[\pi_0(i_0)/\pi_m(i_m)]\prod_{k=1}^m[\pi_k(i_k)/\pi_k(i_{k-1})]$. Substituting $\pi_k(i)=e^{-\beta E_k(i)}/Z_k$ and collecting terms gives $\log(P_F/P_R)=\beta[E_m(i_m)-E_0(i_0)-Q_{\mathrm{in}}]+\log(Z_m/Z_0)=\beta(W-\Delta F)$ by [F3].

The reversed quench at stage $k$ occurs at state $i_{k-1}$, so its work term is $E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})-E_k(i_{k-1})=-[E_k(i_{k-1})-E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})]$; summing proves $W_R(\omega^R)=-W(\omega)$. Summing the path ratio over the finite set of paths with $W=w$ proves the stated distribution identity.

thm-tdmath-compact-continuous-mixture-at.title: Attainment and finite support for compact continuous mixtures

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, complete author-hosted lecture text
references.locator: Complete author-hosted HTML chapter read; §§1.2–1.4, finite canonical and microcanonical ensemble conventions.

references.title: Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics
references.locator: Complete 635-page lecture notes retrieved and read; §§4.2–4.6, pp.192–217, ensembles, microcanonical phase space, quantum density matrices, and traces.

thm-tdmath-compact-continuous-mixture-at.statement: Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty compact, $d\ge1$, and $a:K\to\mathbb R$ continuous. Define $a_{\rm mix}$ as in [[def-tdmath-mixture-generator-space-and-energy]]. Then for every $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$ the infimum defining $a_{\rm mix}(x)$ is attained by a Borel probability measure supported on at most $d+1$ points. The function $a_{\rm mix}$ is lower semicontinuous and convex on $\operatorname{conv}K$, and is the greatest convex function on $\operatorname{conv}K$ bounded above by $a$ on $K$. Minimizing over all Borel probabilities on $K$ gives the same attained value as minimizing over finite mixtures. This is a mathematical compactness result; it makes no phase-preparation or equilibrium postulate.
thm-tdmath-compact-continuous-mixture-at.proof:
**Given:** The data in [A1] and the mixture definitions in [F1].

1.1 Define $\Phi(y)=(y,a(y))\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$ and $G=\Phi(K)$. The map $\Phi$ is continuous. The set $G$ is bounded because $\Phi[K]$ is bounded on compact $K$; it is closed because from any convergent sequence $\Phi(y_n)$, [F3] gives a subsequence $y_{n_j}\to y\in K$, and continuity gives $\Phi(y_{n_j})\to\Phi(y)$. Thus [F3] makes $G$ compact. [A1, F3, algebra]

2.1 Any finite convex combination of more than $d+2$ points of $G\subset\mathbb R^{d+1}$ has an affine dependence: there are coefficients $c_i$, not all zero, with $\sum_i c_i=0$ and $\sum_i c_i g_i=0$. Both signs occur. If its positive weights are $\theta_i$, replacing them by $\theta_i-tc_i$, where $t=\min_{c_i>0}\theta_i/c_i$, preserves their sum and combination, keeps them nonnegative, and makes at least one zero. Repeating gives at most $d+2$ points. Pad shorter combinations by zero weights and repeat any fixed point of nonempty $G$. It follows that $\operatorname{conv}G$ is the continuous image of the compact finite-dimensional parameter set $G^{d+2}\times\Delta_{d+2}$, where $\Delta_{d+2}=\{\theta_i\ge0:\sum_i\theta_i=1\}$. This set is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F3]; the same sequential argument as in 1.1 shows its image is compact. [A1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$. Its fiber $F_x=\{r:(x,r)\in\operatorname{conv}G\}$ is nonempty, since each finite convex combination of generators gives such a point, and compact, since it is a closed section of compact $\operatorname{conv}G$. Therefore [F4] gives a minimum $r_x$. A convex-combination representation of $(x,r_x)$ by points $(y_i,a(y_i))$ defines a finite atomic Borel probability $P_x$ with barycenter $x$ and energy $r_x$. [A1, F1, F3, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 Conversely, for any Borel probability $P$ on $K$, the vector-valued map $\Phi$ is bounded and coordinatewise integrable by [F2]. Its integral is in $\operatorname{conv}G$: for each $\epsilon>0$, uniform continuity of $\Phi$ gives a finite Borel partition of $K$ whose pieces have image diameter at most $\epsilon$. Choose a point in each nonempty piece and weight it by that piece's $P$-mass. The resulting finite convex combination differs coordinatewise from $\int\Phi\,dP$ by at most $\epsilon$; as $\operatorname{conv}G$ is closed by step 2.1, the integral belongs to it. If $\bar y(P)=x$, then $(x,\bar a(P))\in\operatorname{conv}G$, so $\bar a(P)\ge r_x$. Together with step 3.1 this proves that the all-measure infimum equals $r_x$ and is attained by $P_x$. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 To prove lower semicontinuity, let $x_n\to x$ in $\operatorname{conv}K$ and pass to a subsequence along which $a_{\rm mix}(x_n)$ tends to its liminf. The values lie between $\min_K a$ and $\max_K a$, attained by [F4], so a further subsequence of $(x_n,a_{\rm mix}(x_n))$ converges. Each pair lies in the compact set $\operatorname{conv}G$ by step 4.1; its limit is therefore $(x,r)\in\operatorname{conv}G$. The minimum in the fiber at $x$ satisfies $a_{\rm mix}(x)\le r=\liminf_n a_{\rm mix}(x_n)$. [A1, F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1]

5.2 Combine minimizers $P_x$ and $P_z$ with weights $s$ and $1-s$, $0\le s\le1$. The combined finite measure has barycenter $sx+(1-s)z$ and energy $s a_{\rm mix}(x)+(1-s)a_{\rm mix}(z)$. By step 4.1, the minimum at the combined barycenter is no greater than this value. Hence $a_{\rm mix}$ is convex. [F1, step 3.1, step 4.1]

5.3 The support reduction in 2.1 first gives at most $d+2$ atoms. If an optimal representation has more than $d+1$ positive weights, the points $y_i\in\mathbb R^d$ have an affine dependence $\sum_i c_i y_i=0$, $\sum_i c_i=0$. For sufficiently small positive $t$, both weight lists $\theta_i\pm t c_i$ remain nonnegative and preserve the barycenter. If $\sum_i c_i a(y_i)\ne0$, one of these lists strictly lowers energy, contradicting optimality; hence this sum is zero. Increase $t$ in one sign to the first value at which a positive coefficient becomes zero. The new weights preserve barycenter and energy and still attain the minimum; iteration leaves at most $d+1$ positive weights. [A1, F1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Finally, let $g$ be any convex function on $\operatorname{conv}K$ with $g(y)\le a(y)$ for $y\in K$. For the finite optimal measure from 4.1, finite Jensen (obtained by iterating the two-point convexity inequality) gives $g(x)\le\sum_i\theta_i g(y_i)\le\sum_i\theta_i a(y_i)=a_{\rm mix}(x)$. Since $a_{\rm mix}(y)\le a(y)$ for $y\in K$ by the point mass at $y$, it is itself such a convex minorant and dominates every other one. [F1, step 5.2, step 5.3, algebra] ∎

ex-tdmath-correlated-pair-mutual-informa.statement: Let $M,R\in\{0,1\}$ have joint probabilities $p(0,0)=p(1,1)=1/2$ and $p(0,1)=p(1,0)=0$. Then $H(M)=H(R)=\log2$, $H(M,R)=\log2$, $H(M|R)=0$, and $I(M;R)=\log2$.
ex-tdmath-correlated-pair-mutual-informa.proof:
**Given:** The finite joint probability law in [A1].

1.1 Both marginals are uniform, so their entropies are $-2(1/2)\log(1/2)=\log2$. The joint law has two positive entries of size $1/2$, so $H(M,R)=\log2$. [A1, algebra]

2.1 Conditional on either value of $R$, $M$ is determined, so its conditional law has one probability $1$ and one $0$; therefore $H(M|R)=0$. Substituting these values into [F1] gives $I(M;R)=\log2$. [F1, F2, A1, step 1.1] ∎
