ex-tdmath-countable-partition-divergence.statement: Take $I=\mathbb N$, $E_n=0$, and $g_n=1$ for every $n$. The energy list is bounded below, but $Z(\beta)=+\infty$ for every real $\beta$, so this model has no normalized canonical law.
ex-tdmath-countable-partition-divergence.proof:
**Given:** The countable model in [F1] with the data in [A1].

1.1 Every summand is $g_ne^{-\beta E_n}=1$, so the first $N$ terms sum to $N$ for every $N$; their supremum is infinite. [F1, A1, algebra]

2.1 Thus $Z(\beta)=+\infty$, which violates the finite-normalization condition in [F1]; no normalized canonical probabilities $p_n$ are defined. [F1, step 1.1] ∎

thm-tdmath-summable-canonical-differenti.title: Summable canonical differentiation

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, author-hosted complete HTML chapter text
references.locator: Full author-hosted HTML chapter text read; §§1.3–1.4, printed pp.17–30, for canonical and grand-canonical normalizations and responses.

references.title: Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics (work in progress, dated 12 October 2026)
references.locator: Complete 635-page PDF retrieved; §§4.2–4.6, printed pp.192–217, for microcanonical, canonical, quantum trace and grand-canonical constructions.

thm-tdmath-summable-canonical-differenti.statement: Let $I,E_i,g_i,J,Z$ be as in [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]. Suppose that for every compact interval $K\subset J$ there is a summable sequence $a_i\ge0$ such that $g_i(1+|E_i|^2)\exp(-\beta E_i)\le a_i$ for every $i\in I$ and $\beta\in K$. Then $Z$ is positive, finite, and $C^2$ on $J$, with $Z'(\beta)=-\sum_i g_iE_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ and $Z''(\beta)=\sum_i g_iE_i^2\exp(-\beta E_i)$. The probabilities $p_i$ are normalized; their mean $\bar E$ and variance are finite and satisfy $-\partial_\beta\log Z=\bar E$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log Z=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$. Moreover $H_g(p)=\log Z+\beta\bar E$, and its defining series is absolutely convergent.
thm-tdmath-summable-canonical-differenti.proof:
**Given:** The countable canonical model and the local summable envelope in the statement.

1.1 On a compact interval $K\subset J$, let $Z_N$, $D_N$, and $Q_N$ be the first $N$ partial sums of $\sum_i g_i e^{-\beta E_i}$, $-\sum_i g_iE_ie^{-\beta E_i}$, and $\sum_i g_iE_i^2e^{-\beta E_i}$. Since $|E_i|^r\le1+|E_i|^2$ for $r=0,1,2$, each tail is bounded uniformly on $K$ by the corresponding tail of $\sum_i a_i$, which tends to zero [A1]. Thus all three sequences converge uniformly; call their limits $Z,D,Q$. Each finite partial sum has the displayed derivatives by the chain rule [F5] and the exponential derivative [F2]. Each partial sum is continuous, so the uniform limits are continuous by the $\varepsilon/3$ definition of continuity. [F1, A1, F2, F5]

2.1 For an interior $\beta$ and sufficiently small $h\ne0$, apply [F4] to $Z_N$ on the interval with endpoints $\beta$ and $\beta+h$: its difference quotient is $D_N(\xi_{N,h})$ for some intermediate $\xi_{N,h}$. Choose $N=N(h)$ so that $\sup_K|Z_N-Z|<h^2$ and $\sup_K|D_N-D|<|h|$. The difference quotient for $Z$ then differs from $D(\beta)$ by at most $2|h|+|h|+\sup_{|t-\beta|\le|h|}|D(t)-D(\beta)|$, which tends to zero by continuity of $D$. Hence $Z'=D$. Applying the same argument to $D_N$ and $Q_N$ proves $D'=Q$, so the displayed derivatives hold. [F2, F4, F5, step 1.1]

3.1 The summands of $Z$ are positive and at least one is present, hence $0<Z<\infty$ on $K$; summing the definition of $p_i$ gives $\sum_i p_i=1$. The envelope also gives $\sum_i p_i|E_i|$ and $\sum_i p_iE_i^2$ finite. Differentiating $\log Z$ using [F3] yields $-Z'/Z=\bar E$ and $Z''/Z-(Z'/Z)^2=\langle E^2\rangle-\bar E^2=\operatorname{Var}_\beta(E)$. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1]

4.1 Since $p_i/g_i=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$, its logarithm is $-\beta E_i-\log Z$. The finite first moment makes $\sum_i p_i|\log(p_i/g_i)|\le |\beta|\sum_i p_i|E_i|+|\log Z|\sum_i p_i<\infty$; summing the identity gives $H_g=\beta\bar E+\log Z$. [F1, F2, F3, step 3.1] ∎

ex-tdmath-finite-ensemble-mismatch.title: A finite canonical law differs from a narrow-shell microcanonical law

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, author-hosted complete HTML chapter text
references.locator: Full author-hosted HTML chapter text read; canonical ensemble and finite-state examples §§1.2–1.3, printed pp.2–26.

references.title: Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics (work in progress, dated 12 October 2026)
references.locator: Complete 635-page PDF retrieved; probability §§1.3–1.5 pp.8–30 and ensemble examples §§4.2–4.6 pp.192–217.

ex-tdmath-finite-ensemble-mismatch.statement: Let a two-state model have energies $0$ and $\varepsilon>0$, with unit state weights and $\beta>0$. Adopt the finite-shell convention that the microcanonical law is uniform over states whose energy lies in $[0,\Delta)$ when the shell is nonempty. For $0<\Delta<\varepsilon$, that shell contains only the ground state, whereas the canonical law assigns the excited state probability $e^{-\beta\varepsilon}/(1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon})>0$. Thus the two finite-ensemble laws differ.
ex-tdmath-finite-ensemble-mismatch.proof:
**Given:** The finite model and shell convention in [A1].

1.1 The canonical partition sum is $1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon}$; its excited probability is $e^{-\beta\varepsilon}/(1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon})$, strictly positive because the exponential is positive. [F1, F2, A1]

2.1 The shell condition $0\le E_i<\Delta$ includes the state of energy zero and excludes the state of energy $\varepsilon$, since $\Delta<\varepsilon$. Uniform weighting of this one-state shell gives excited probability zero, which differs from step 1.1. [A1, step 1.1] ∎

thm-tdmath-general-trace-gibbs-model.title: Trace-class Gibbs normalization for a semibounded self-adjoint operator

references.title: Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics (work in progress, dated 12 October 2026)
references.locator: Complete 635-page PDF retrieved; ensembles and traces §§4.2–4.6 pp.192–217; Bose/Fermi models §§5.6–5.7 pp.277–303; 1D Ising §6.2.2 pp.330–333.

thm-tdmath-general-trace-gibbs-model.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $A$ be self-adjoint with regular Borel projection-valued measure $E$ from [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], with $E((-\infty,a))=0$ for finite $a\in\mathbb R$. For each $\gamma>0$, define the bounded Gibbs operator $K_\gamma:=\Phi_E(f_\gamma)$ using the bounded Borel PVM integral of [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], where $f_\gamma(\lambda)=e^{-\gamma\lambda}$ for $\lambda\ge a$ and $f_\gamma(\lambda)=e^{-\gamma a}$ for $\lambda<a$. Fix $\beta>0$ and suppose $K_\beta$ is trace class in the sense of [[def-trace-class-operator]]. Then $K_\beta$ is injective and has a finite or countable orthonormal basis $(u_j)$ of $\mathcal H$ with $Au_j=E_ju_j$, $E_j\ge a$, and $K_\beta u_j=e^{-\beta E_j}u_j$. Its partition function $Z_\beta:=\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta=\sum_j e^{-\beta E_j}$ is positive and finite, and $\rho_\beta:=K_\beta/Z_\beta$ is positive with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_\beta=1$. For every $B\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta B)=\sum_j(e^{-\beta E_j}/Z_\beta)\langle Bu_j,u_j\rangle$ absolutely. Further, let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and suppose that for every compact $C\subset J$ there is a summable family $a_j\ge0$ with $(1+|E_j|^2)e^{-\gamma E_j}\le a_j$ for all $j$ and $\gamma\in C$. Then for each $\gamma\in J$, $K_\gamma$ is trace class with partition function $Z_\gamma:=\operatorname{Tr}K_\gamma=\sum_j e^{-\gamma E_j}$. With $p_j(\gamma):=e^{-\gamma E_j}/Z_\gamma$, define $\bar E_\gamma:=\sum_jp_j(\gamma)E_j$, $\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(E):=\sum_jp_j(\gamma)(E_j-\bar E_\gamma)^2$, and $S_\gamma:=-\sum_jp_j(\gamma)\log p_j(\gamma)$. These quantities are finite and satisfy $-\partial_\gamma\log Z_\gamma=\bar E_\gamma$, $\partial_\gamma^2\log Z_\gamma=\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(E)$, and $S_\gamma=\log Z_\gamma+\gamma\bar E_\gamma$ as in [[thm-tdmath-summable-canonical-differentiation]]. Countable nonnegative sums use the finite-subsum supremum convention of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]].
thm-tdmath-general-trace-gibbs-model.proof:
**Given:** AC, a nonzero complex Hilbert space, self-adjoint semibounded $A$, its spectral PVM, a parameter $\beta>0$, and trace-class $K_\beta$.

1.1 Since $\beta>0$, $-\beta\lambda\le-\beta a$ for $\lambda\ge a$; strict increase and positivity from [F11] show that $f_\beta$ is bounded and strictly positive. Each branch is continuous and their values agree at $a$, so $f_\beta$ is Borel. For each $n$, partition its bounded range into finitely many intervals of length at most $1/n$ and take their Borel preimages; choosing a nonnegative value in each interval gives a nonnegative real simple $s_n$ converging uniformly to $f_\beta$. By [F13], $T_n:=\int s_n\,dE$ is a finite real linear combination of self-adjoint projections, hence self-adjoint and has nonnegative quadratic form. By [F2], $T_n\to K_\beta$ in operator norm. Therefore $\langle K_\beta x,y\rangle=\langle x,K_\beta y\rangle$ and $\langle K_\beta x,x\rangle\ge0$ by [F14] and passage to the limit, so $K_\beta$ is self-adjoint and positive. If $K_\beta x=0$, [F2] gives $\int f_\beta^2dE_x=0$. For each $n\ge1$, $f_\beta\ge1/n$ on $C_n:=\{\lambda:f_\beta(\lambda)\ge1/n\}$; [F16] gives $0=\int f_\beta^2dE_x\ge n^{-2}E_x(C_n)$, so $E_x(C_n)=0$. The sets $C_n$ increase to $\mathbb R$; set $D_1=C_1$ and $D_n=C_n\setminus C_{n-1}$ for $n>1$. They are disjoint, cover $\mathbb R$, and satisfy $E_x(D_n)\le E_x(C_n)=0$. Countable additivity in [F13] gives $E_x(\mathbb R)=\sum_nE_x(D_n)=0$, hence $\|x\|=0$ and $K_\beta$ is injective. [A1, F1, F2, F11, F13, F14, F16]

2.1 By the trace-class definition [F4], $K_\beta$ is compact; together with step 1.1 it is compact self-adjoint and positive. Apply [F3]: its nonzero eigenspaces have finite multiplicity and span $(\ker K_\beta)^\perp=\mathcal H$, so AC supplies a finite or countable complete orthonormal family $(u_j)$ of eigenvectors with eigenvalues $\kappa_j>0$. By [F4], $Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta=\sum_j\kappa_j<\infty$; because $\mathcal H\ne0$ and $K_\beta$ is injective, this sum is positive. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 Fix $j$. To justify the constant shift in the calculus, choose bounded simple $s_n\to f_\beta$ uniformly. By [F13], $\int(s_n-\kappa_j)\,dE=\int s_n\,dE-\kappa_jI$; [F2] passes both uniform limits, so $\Phi_E(f_\beta-\kappa_j)=K_\beta-\kappa_jI$. Applying the norm identity in [F2] to this difference and the eigenvector gives $\int|f_\beta-\kappa_j|^2dE_{u_j}=\|(K_\beta-\kappa_jI)u_j\|^2=0$. For every $n$, [F16] shows that the set where $|f_\beta-\kappa_j|\ge1/n$ has zero $E_{u_j}$-measure; their union is the complement of the level set. Hence $E_{u_j}$ is supported on $f_\beta^{-1}(\kappa_j)\cap[a,\infty)=\{E_j\}$: injectivity of the exponential gives uniqueness, and [F12] gives $E_j=-\beta^{-1}\log\kappa_j\ge a$. Thus $\int\lambda^2dE_{u_j}=E_j^2<\infty$ and [F1] yields $u_j\in D(A)$ and $Au_j=E_ju_j$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F11, F12, F13, F16, step 2.1]

4.1 The spectral measure of each $u_j$ is the unit mass at $E_j$ by step 3.1. Hence $\|(I-E(\{E_j\}))u_j\|^2=E_{u_j}(\mathbb R\setminus\{E_j\})=0$, so $E(\{E_j\})u_j=u_j$; for Borel $D$ not containing $E_j$, $E(D)u_j=E(D)E(\{E_j\})u_j=E(\varnothing)u_j=0$ by [F13]. For every $\gamma>0$, choose nonnegative simple $s_n\to f_\gamma$ uniformly as in step 1.1. In each disjoint normal form, [F13] then gives $(\int s_n\,dE)u_j=s_n(E_j)u_j$; the uniform-limit clause of [F2] yields $K_\gamma u_j=f_\gamma(E_j)u_j=e^{-\gamma E_j}u_j$. Fix $\gamma\in J$ and enumerate that basis; let $P_N$ project onto its first $N$ vectors, taking $P_N=I$ once a finite basis is exhausted. Parseval gives $\|P_Nx\|\le\|x\|$, so $K_\gamma P_N$ is bounded and finite rank. Fix the summable envelope $a_j$ for $\{\gamma\}\subset J$; every finite subsum of $t_j:=e^{-\gamma E_j}$ is at most the corresponding sum of $a_j$, hence $S:=\sum_jt_j<\infty$ by the finite-subsum definition [F6]. This sum is positive because the basis is nonempty and every term is positive. For $\varepsilon>0$, choose a finite set $F$ with $S-\varepsilon<\sum_{j\in F}t_j$; once $N$ contains $F$, every finite tail subsum is at most $S-\sum_{j\in F}t_j<\varepsilon$, so $\sum_{j>N}t_j\to0$. Again by Parseval, $$\|(K_\gamma-K_\gamma P_N)x\|^2=\sum_{j>N}e^{-2\gamma E_j}|\langle x,u_j\rangle|^2\le\Bigl(\sum_{j>N}e^{-\gamma E_j}\Bigr)^2\|x\|^2,$$ so $K_\gamma P_N$ converges to $K_\gamma$ in operator norm. For $t_j=e^{-\gamma E_j}$ its finite diagonal expansion is $K_\gamma P_Nx=\sum_{j\le N}t_j\langle x,u_j\rangle u_j$; orthonormality and [F8] give $\langle K_\gamma P_Nx,y\rangle=\langle x,K_\gamma P_Ny\rangle$ and $\langle K_\gamma P_Nx,x\rangle=\sum_{j\le N}t_j|\langle x,u_j\rangle|^2\ge0$. Thus each truncation is self-adjoint and positive, and [F14] plus operator-norm convergence preserves both properties. It is compact by [F15], since the truncations are bounded finite-rank operators and $\mathcal H$ is Banach. Thus $K_\gamma$ is compact self-adjoint and positive. Its absolute value is $K_\gamma$, by the unique positive square-root definition in [F9]. If $K_\gamma x=\lambda x$, taking coordinates in the complete basis gives $(t_j-\lambda)\langle x,u_j\rangle=0$ for every $j$; thus its eigenvalues and their multiplicities are exactly the diagonal values $t_j$. Hence [F9] identifies its positive singular values, with multiplicity, as the list $(t_j)$. Their finite subsums are bounded by $\sum_j a_j$, so the trace-class definition [F4] applies and gives $\operatorname{Tr}K_\gamma=\sum_j t_j$. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F6, F8, F9, F10, F13, F14, F15, step 1.1, step 3.1]

5.1 At the fixed $\beta$, $\rho_\beta=K_\beta/Z_\beta$ is positive trace class and [F5] gives $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_\beta=Z_\beta^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta=1$. For each $\gamma\in J$, $\rho_\gamma=K_\gamma/Z_\gamma$ likewise has trace one; its eigenvalues $p_j=e^{-\gamma E_j}/Z_\gamma$ form the canonical law, so [F6] gives the finite mean, variance, and identity $-\sum_jp_j\log p_j=\log Z_\gamma+\gamma\sum_jp_jE_j$. [A1, F5, F6, step 2.1, step 4.1]

6.1 For bounded $B$, [F5] makes $\rho_\beta B$ and $B\rho_\beta$ trace class and [F7] gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta B)=\operatorname{Tr}(B\rho_\beta)$. Evaluate the second trace in the complete basis $(u_j)$: $\operatorname{Tr}(B\rho_\beta)=\sum_j\langle B\rho_\beta u_j,u_j\rangle=\sum_jp_j\langle Bu_j,u_j\rangle$, where [F8] and real $p_j$ justify pulling the scalar out. This series is absolutely convergent since $|\langle Bu_j,u_j\rangle|\le\|B\|$ and $\sum_jp_j=1$. [A1, A2, F3, F5, F7, F8, step 5.1] ∎

ex-tdmath-two-level-canonical-fluctuatio.title: Canonical mean and variance for a two-level system

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, author-hosted complete HTML chapter text
references.locator: Full author-hosted HTML chapter text read; canonical ensemble and finite-state examples §§1.2–1.3, printed pp.2–26.

references.title: Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics (work in progress, dated 12 October 2026)
references.locator: Complete 635-page PDF retrieved; probability §§1.3–1.5 pp.8–30 and ensemble examples §§4.2–4.6 pp.192–217.

ex-tdmath-two-level-canonical-fluctuatio.statement: Let the state set be $\{0,1\}$, with energies $E_0=0$, $E_1=\varepsilon>0$, unit weights, and $\beta>0$. Writing $q=e^{-\beta\varepsilon}$, the excited-state probability is $q/(1+q)$, the mean energy is $\varepsilon q/(1+q)$, and the energy variance is $\varepsilon^2q/(1+q)^2>0$.
ex-tdmath-two-level-canonical-fluctuatio.proof:
**Given:** The finite canonical model [F1] with data [A1].

1.1 Direct summation gives $Z=1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon}=1+q$, hence $p_1=q/(1+q)$ and $p_0=1/(1+q)$. [F1, A1, algebra]

2.1 The finite weighted sum gives $\bar E=\varepsilon p_1=\varepsilon q/(1+q)$. The second centered moment is $p_0(0-\bar E)^2+p_1(\varepsilon-\bar E)^2=\varepsilon^2q/(1+q)^2$, which is positive because $q\in(0,1)$. The values also agree with the finite-list derivative identities of [F2]. [F1, F2, A1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

lem-tdmath-bose-fermi-mode-fluctuations.title: Single-mode Bose and Fermi occupation fluctuations

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, author-hosted complete HTML chapter text
references.locator: Full author-hosted HTML chapter text read; canonical/grand-canonical ensembles §§1.3–1.4 pp.17–30; two-state model §1.2.3 pp.11–14; 1D Ising §5.3.1 pp.156–157.

references.title: Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics (work in progress, dated 12 October 2026)
references.locator: Complete 635-page PDF retrieved; ensembles and traces §§4.2–4.6 pp.192–217; Bose/Fermi models §§5.6–5.7 pp.277–303; 1D Ising §6.2.2 pp.330–333.

lem-tdmath-bose-fermi-mode-fluctuations.statement: For $q\in(0,1)$, the bosonic geometric law on $n\in\mathbb N_0$ with weights $(1-q)q^n$ has mean $q/(1-q)$ and variance $q/(1-q)^2=\mathbb E[n](1+\mathbb E[n])$; its relative standard deviation tends to $1$ as $q\uparrow1$. The fermionic two-state law on $n\in\{0,1\}$ with weights $1/(1+q)$ and $q/(1+q)$ has mean $q/(1+q)$ and variance $q/(1+q)^2=\mathbb E[n](1-\mathbb E[n])$. Here Bose and Fermi name these explicitly specified counting laws; no claim about a physical preparation is made.
lem-tdmath-bose-fermi-mode-fluctuations.proof:
**Given:** The geometric and two-state laws with $q\in(0,1)$.

1.1 Let $S_N=\sum_{n=0}^Nq^n$. Multiplying this finite sum by $1-q$ gives $(1-q)S_N=1-q^{N+1}$. Since $q=e^{-\gamma}$ for $\gamma>0$, [F5] gives $q^{N+1}\to0$; hence $Z=(1-q)^{-1}$ and the weights $(1-q)q^n$ sum to one. On a compact $\gamma$-interval $[b,B]\subset(0,\infty)$, set $a_n=(1+n^2)e^{-bn}$. Then $a_{n+1}/a_n=e^{-b}(1+(n+1)^2)/(1+n^2)\to e^{-b}<1$. Choose $c$ with $e^{-b}<c<1$; for all sufficiently large $n$, $a_{n+1}\le ca_n$, so the tail is bounded by a convergent geometric series. Thus $\sum_n(1+n^2)e^{-\gamma n}\le\sum_na_n<\infty$, which is the local envelope required by [F1]. [A1, F1, F3, F5, algebra]

1.2 The fermionic partition sum is $1+q$; its two probabilities are $1/(1+q)$ and $q/(1+q)$. Their finite weighted sums give mean $q/(1+q)$ and variance $q/(1+q)^2$, equal to the mean times one minus the mean. [A1, F2, F3]

2.1 With $Z(\gamma)=(1-e^{-\gamma})^{-1}$, [F1] gives $\mathbb E n=-\partial_\gamma\log Z=q/(1-q)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(n)=\partial_\gamma^2\log Z=q/(1-q)^2$. Substitution $q=e^{-\gamma}$ and [F4] justify the parameter derivatives. Therefore $\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(n)}/\mathbb E n=1/\sqrt q\to1$ as $q\uparrow1$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 These are calculations for the two specified probability laws only; no independence, physical preparation, or measured fluctuation claim is used. [A1, step 2.1, step 1.2] ∎

thm-tdmath-monotone-convergence.title: Monotone convergence for the measure integral

references.title: Terence Tao, 245A Notes 3: Integration on Abstract Measure Spaces and the Convergence Theorems, full author-hosted lecture text
references.locator: Complete HTML lecture text read; abstract measure spaces, integration, Fatou, monotone convergence, dominated convergence, and the L1 convergence argument.

thm-tdmath-monotone-convergence.statement: Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable with $f_n\le f_{n+1}$ and $f_n\to f$ pointwise. Then $\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu$, including infinite values. Also, for measurable $f,g\ge0$, $\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu$. For every $c\ge0$, $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$; the integral is also linear on real integrable functions.
thm-tdmath-monotone-convergence.proof:
**Given:** A measure space and a pointwise increasing sequence $0\le f_n\uparrow f$.

1.1 The simple minorants of $f_n$ are also minorants of $f_{n+1}$, so their integral suprema increase. Each is at most $\int f$; hence $L:=\lim_n\int f_n$ exists in $[0,\infty]$ and $L\le\int f$. [F1, A2]

2.1 Fix a nonnegative simple $s\le f$ and $0<t<1$. The measurable sets $A_n:=\{f_n\ge ts\}$ increase and cover $\{s>0\}$, since $f_n(x)\to f(x)\ge s(x)>ts(x)$ there. Write $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{B_j}$ in disjoint level form. For each $c_j>0$, $A_n\cap B_j\uparrow B_j$; countable additivity, applied to successive disjoint differences, gives $\mu(A_n\cap B_j)\uparrow\mu(B_j)$. The finite-sum definition [F2] then gives $\int s\mathbf1_{A_n}\uparrow\int s$. As $f_n\ge ts\mathbf1_{A_n}$, monotonicity and homogeneity of the simple integral imply $L\ge t\int s$. Let $t\uparrow1$ and take the supremum over $s\le f$; [F1, F3] give $L\ge\int f$. Together with step 1.1 this proves monotone convergence. [F1, F2, F3, A1, A2, step 1.1]

2.2 For nonnegative measurable $f$, define $s_n:=2^{-n}\sum_{k=1}^{n2^n}\mathbf1_{\{f\ge k2^{-n}\}}$. Each $s_n$ is a finite-valued measurable simple function. Every threshold counted in $s_n$ is also counted at the even-index threshold in $s_{n+1}$, so $s_n\le s_{n+1}$. If $f(x)<\infty$, once $n>f(x)$ the mesh gives $0\le f(x)-s_n(x)<2^{-n}$; if $f(x)=\infty$, then $s_n(x)=n$. Thus $s_n\uparrow f$. Define $t_n:=2^{-n}\sum_{k=1}^{n2^n}\mathbf1_{\{g\ge k2^{-n}\}}$; the same threshold and mesh argument shows $t_n\uparrow g$. Apply step 1.1 to $s_n$, $t_n$, and $s_n+t_n$. Refine their finitely many level sets to the finite partition of intersections $B_j\cap C_k$; regrouping the resulting sums by [F2] gives $\int(s_n+t_n)=\int s_n+\int t_n$. Passing to the three monotone limits proves $\int(f+g)=\int f+\int g$. [F1, F2, A1, step 1.1]

3.1 For $c>0$, simple minorants of $cf$ are exactly $c$ times simple minorants of $f$, so the supremum definition gives $\int cf=c\int f$; for $c=0$ both sides are zero. If an integrable real function is expressed as $u-v$ with $u,v\ge0$ integrable, the value $\int u-\int v$ is independent of the expression: $u-v=u'-v'$ implies $u+v'=u'+v$, and step 2.2 equates the finite sums of integrals. The definition using positive and negative parts is one such expression, so signed integrals are linear. [F1, F2, step 2.2] ∎

lem-tdmath-fatou.title: Fatou's lemma

references.title: Terence Tao, 245A Notes 3: Integration on Abstract Measure Spaces and the Convergence Theorems, full author-hosted lecture text
references.locator: Complete HTML lecture text read; abstract measure spaces, integration, Fatou, monotone convergence, dominated convergence, and the L1 convergence argument.

lem-tdmath-fatou.statement: Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable. Then $\int\liminf_{n\to\infty} f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu$.
lem-tdmath-fatou.proof:
**Given:** A measure space and measurable $f_n\ge0$.

1.1 Set $h_k:=\inf_{n\ge k}f_n$. For each real $a$, $\{h_k<a\}=\bigcup_{n\ge k}\{f_n<a\}$, so $h_k$ is measurable by the sigma-algebra closure in [F1]. The sequence $h_k$ is increasing and its pointwise limit is $\liminf_n f_n$, which is measurable since $\{\lim_kh_k>a\}=\bigcup_k\{h_k>a\}$. [F1, A1]

2.1 For every $n\ge k$, monotonicity gives $\int h_k\le\int f_n$, so $\int h_k\le\inf_{n\ge k}\int f_n$. Taking $k\to\infty$ and applying monotone convergence to $h_k$ yields $\int\liminf f_n=\lim_k\int h_k\le\lim_k\inf_{n\ge k}\int f_n=\liminf_n\int f_n$. [F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

lem-tdmath-finite-ground-degeneracy.title: Finite ground-state degeneracy entropy limit

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, author-hosted complete HTML chapter text
references.locator: Full author-hosted HTML chapter text read; canonical/grand-canonical ensembles §§1.3–1.4 pp.17–30; two-state model §1.2.3 pp.11–14; 1D Ising §5.3.1 pp.156–157.

references.title: Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics (work in progress, dated 12 October 2026)
references.locator: Complete 635-page PDF retrieved; ensembles and traces §§4.2–4.6 pp.192–217; Bose/Fermi models §§5.6–5.7 pp.277–303; 1D Ising §6.2.2 pp.330–333.

lem-tdmath-finite-ground-degeneracy.statement: Let a finite canonical model have energies $E_i$, ground energy $E_0$, and exactly $g\ge1$ states at $E_0$, with every other energy strictly larger. As $\beta\to+\infty$, each ground-state probability tends to $1/g$, each excited-state probability tends to zero, and the Shannon entropy $-\sum_i p_i(\beta)\log p_i(\beta)$ tends to $\log g$. This is a finite-model statement only.
lem-tdmath-finite-ground-degeneracy.proof:
**Given:** A finite energy list with ground energy $E_0$, degeneracy $g\ge1$, and positive gaps for all other states.

1.1 Factor $e^{-\beta E_0}$ from the partition sum to obtain $Z=e^{-\beta E_0}(g+\sum_{i:E_i>E_0}e^{-\beta(E_i-E_0)})$. Every gap is positive, and there are finitely many, so the parenthesized sum tends to $g$. Thus each ground probability tends to $1/g$ and every excited probability tends to zero. [A1, F1, F2]

2.1 Ground-state entropy terms tend to $-g(1/g)\log(1/g)=\log g$. For an excited state with gap $\Delta_i>0$, step 1.1 gives $p_i=O(e^{-\beta\Delta_i})$ and $\log p_i=-\beta\Delta_i-\log D(\beta)$, where $D(\beta):=g+\sum_{j:E_j>E_0}e^{-\beta(E_j-E_0)}\to g>0$ by step 1.1, so $\log D(\beta)$ is bounded by continuity of $\log$; hence $|p_i\log p_i|=O((1+\beta)e^{-\beta\Delta_i})\to0$ by [F3]. The excited sum is finite, so its limit is zero and the total entropy tends to $\log g$. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

thm-tdmath-limiting-derivative-and-conce.title: Limiting derivative and concentration

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, author-hosted complete HTML chapter text
references.locator: Full author-hosted HTML chapter text read; canonical/grand-canonical ensembles §§1.3–1.4 pp.17–30; two-state model §1.2.3 pp.11–14; 1D Ising §5.3.1 pp.156–157.

references.title: Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics (work in progress, dated 12 October 2026)
references.locator: Complete 635-page PDF retrieved; ensembles and traces §§4.2–4.6 pp.192–217; Bose/Fermi models §§5.6–5.7 pp.277–303; 1D Ising §6.2.2 pp.330–333.

thm-tdmath-limiting-derivative-and-conce.statement: For the lattice models of [[thm-tdmath-finite-range-lattice-pressure-limit]], write $p_L(\gamma)=L^{-d}\log Z_L(\gamma)$ and let $p(\gamma)=\lim_Lp_L(\gamma)$ on an open interval $J\subseteq(0,\infty)$. At finite $L$, use the canonical law $\mathbb P_{\gamma,L}(s):=e^{-\gamma H_L(s)}/Z_L(\gamma)$ and its finite expectation $\mathbb E_{\gamma,L}$. If $p$ is differentiable at $\beta\in J$, then $\mathbb E_{\beta,L}[H_L]/L^d\to e:=-p'(\beta)$. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there are $c>0$ and $L_0$ such that for $L\ge L_0$, $\mathbb P_{\beta,L}(|H_L/L^d-e|\ge\varepsilon)\le2e^{-cL^d}$. No energy-density limit is asserted at a nondifferentiability point.
thm-tdmath-limiting-derivative-and-conce.proof:
**Given:** The finite-volume lattice models, their canonical probabilities, pointwise convergence $p_L\to p$ on $J$, and differentiability of $p$ at $\beta$.

1.1 Differentiating the finite sum gives $p_L'=-L^{-d}\mathbb E_{\beta,L}H_L$ and $p_L''=L^{-d}\operatorname{Var}_{\beta,L}(H_L)\ge0$. Thus $p_L$ is convex. Passing the two-point convexity inequality to the pointwise limit shows that $p$ is convex too. [A1, F2, F3, F4]

1.2 Fix $t>0$ small enough that $\beta\pm t\in J$. For the upper tail, the pointwise inequality $\mathbf1_{\{H_L\ge L^d(e+\varepsilon)\}}\le e^{t(H_L-L^d(e+\varepsilon))}$ and finite summation give $\mathbb P(H_L/L^d\ge e+\varepsilon)\le\exp\{L^d[p_L(\beta-t)-p_L(\beta)-t(e+\varepsilon)]\}$. Differentiability of $p$ and $e=-p'(\beta)$ imply $p(\beta-t)=p(\beta)+te+o(t)$; choose $t$ so the bracket's limit is at most $-3t\varepsilon/4$. Pointwise convergence at $\beta-t$ and $\beta$ then makes the bracket at most $-t\varepsilon/2$ for all sufficiently large $L$. [A1, F1, F2, F4]

2.1 For any small $h>0$ with $\beta\pm h\in J$, convexity and differentiability of $p_L$ give $[p_L(\beta)-p_L(\beta-h)]/h\le p_L'(\beta)\le[p_L(\beta+h)-p_L(\beta)]/h$. Take lower and upper limits in $L$, use [F1], then let $h\downarrow0$; differentiability of $p$ forces $p_L'(\beta)\to p'(\beta)$. The identity in step 1.1 yields the claimed mean limit. [A1, F1, F5, step 1.1]

2.2 For the lower tail use $\mathbf1_{\{H_L\le L^d(e-\varepsilon)\}}\le e^{-t(H_L-L^d(e-\varepsilon))}$; its expectation is $\exp\{L^d[p_L(\beta+t)-p_L(\beta)+t(e-\varepsilon)]\}$. Since $p(\beta+t)=p(\beta)-te+o(t)$, possibly reducing $t$ and increasing $L_0$ makes this at most $e^{-L^dt\varepsilon/2}$. Adding both tail bounds yields the result with $c=t\varepsilon/2$. [A1, F1, F2, F4, step 1.2]

3.1 Steps 1.2–2.2 bound the two tails whose union is $\{|H_L/L^d-e|\ge\varepsilon\}$; the theorem is conditional on differentiability of $p$ and does not assert convergence of second derivatives or equivalence for arbitrary observables. [A1, step 1.2, step 2.2] ∎

thm-tdmath-finite-bath-error-bound.title: Finite-bath canonical error bound

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, author-hosted complete HTML chapter text
references.locator: Full author-hosted HTML chapter text read; canonical/grand-canonical ensembles §§1.3–1.4 pp.17–30; two-state model §1.2.3 pp.11–14; 1D Ising §5.3.1 pp.156–157.

references.title: Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics (work in progress, dated 12 October 2026)
references.locator: Complete 635-page PDF retrieved; ensembles and traces §§4.2–4.6 pp.192–217; Bose/Fermi models §§5.6–5.7 pp.277–303; 1D Ising §6.2.2 pp.330–333.

thm-tdmath-finite-bath-error-bound.statement: Let $I$ be a finite nonempty subsystem state set, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $|E_i|\le L$ for $L\ge0$, and let the dimensionless bath entropy $s_B$ be $C^2$ on an open interval $U$ containing $[u_0-L,u_0+L]$, with $|s_B''(u)|\le M$ on that closed interval for $M\ge0$. Use one energy unit for $E_i,u_0,L$, so $\beta=s_B'(u_0)$ has inverse-energy units and $M$ has inverse-energy-squared units; $\delta=ML^2/2$ is dimensionless. Put $Z:=\sum_{j\in I}e^{-\beta E_j}$ and $q_i:=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$. Suppose the joint shell weights induce the normalized subsystem law $p_i:=e^{s_B(u_0-E_i)}/\sum_{j\in I}e^{s_B(u_0-E_j)}$. Then $|s_B(u_0-E_i)-s_B(u_0)+\beta E_i|\le\delta$ for every $i$, and $\sum_i|p_i-q_i|\le e^{2\delta}-1$.
thm-tdmath-finite-bath-error-bound.proof:
**Given:** The finite subsystem, the twice differentiable bath entropy with bounded second derivative, and the stated shell-weight rule.

1.1 Apply [F2] to $s_B$ at $u_0$ with increment $-E_i$. It gives $s_B(u_0-E_i)=s_B(u_0)-\beta E_i+r_i$ where $|r_i|\le M E_i^2/2\le\delta$. [A1, F2]

2.1 The marginal is therefore $p_i=q_i e^{r_i}/C$, where $C:=\sum_jq_je^{r_j}$. The bounds $e^{-\delta}\le e^{r_j}\le e^\delta$ and $\sum_jq_j=1$ imply $e^{-\delta}\le C\le e^\delta$, so $e^{-2\delta}\le p_i/q_i\le e^{2\delta}$. [F1, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 For $x\in[e^{-2\delta},e^{2\delta}]$, $|x-1|\le e^{2\delta}-1$. Thus $\sum_i|p_i-q_i|=\sum_iq_i|p_i/q_i-1|\le(e^{2\delta}-1)\sum_iq_i=e^{2\delta}-1$. The case $\delta=0$ is included and gives equality of the laws. [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

cex-td-clapeyron-zero-volume-jump.title: Equal branch volumes do not give a Clapeyron graph
cex-td-clapeyron-zero-volume-jump.physical_scope: A constructed pair of smooth one-component Gibbs charts with zero molar-volume jump; it shows why the local nonzero-jump hypothesis cannot be omitted and makes no material claim.

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, author-hosted complete lecture notes, §§5.1.1–5.1.2
Konstantin K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Statistical Mechanics, §4.1 First-order phase transitions

cex-td-clapeyron-zero-volume-jump.statement:
Fix $T_0>0$, $p_0>0$, $g_0\in\mathbb R$, $v_0,c,\kappa>0$, and distinct positive molar entropies $s_\alpha,s_\beta$. Use units $g_0\in\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $v_0\in\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, $c\in\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\kappa\in\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}Pa^{-1}}$. On a common open chart define
$$
g_i(T,p)=g_0-s_i(T-T_0)-\frac{c}{2T_0}(T-T_0)^2+v_0(p-p_0)-\frac{\kappa}{2}(p-p_0)^2,
$$
with $i\in\{\alpha,\beta\}$. Let $G_i=n_i g_i$ and adopt $S_i=-\partial_TG_i$, $V_i=\partial_pG_i$, $\mu_i=\partial_{n_i}G_i$, and $U_i=G_i+TS_i-pV_i$. This gives same-tag scaling and smooth local Gibbs charts. At $(T_0,p_0)$ the molar Gibbs values agree and the molar-volume jump is zero; the entropies differ.
cex-td-clapeyron-zero-volume-jump.proof:
1.1 At $(T_0,p_0)$, differentiation gives $S_i/n_i=s_i$, $V_i/n_i=v_0$, and $\mu_i=g_i=g_0$. Also $U_{i,T}=n_i c$, $V_{i,p}=-n_i\kappa$, and $V_{i,T}=0$, so the derivative determinant for $(T,p)\mapsto(U_i,V_i)$ at fixed positive amount is $-n_i^2c\kappa\ne0$. Thus [L1] supplies valid local state charts. The branch equality function is
$$
F(T,p):=g_\beta-g_\alpha=-(s_\beta-s_\alpha)(T-T_0),
$$
whose zero set is $T=T_0$ with every nearby chart pressure permitted. [given, A1, L1, algebra]

2.1 Here $\Delta v=v_\beta-v_\alpha=0$, so the zero set is not the graph of a unique pressure as a function of temperature on an open interval about $T_0$, and the quotient $\Delta s/\Delta v$ is undefined. The nonzero-jump hypothesis of [F1] fails, so this model does not contradict that theorem. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

cex-td-noncompact-phase-mixture-no-attai.title: A noncompact phase domain with no attained mixture maximum
cex-td-noncompact-phase-mixture-no-attai.physical_scope: A constructed continuous concave entropy functional on a noncompact phase-generator domain; it shows that the compactness hypothesis in the mixture-attainment result cannot simply be dropped.

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, author-hosted complete lecture notes, §5.4.3
Konstantin K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Statistical Mechanics, §4.1 First-order phase transitions

cex-td-noncompact-phase-mixture-no-attai.statement:
Let the one-dimensional phase-generator domain be $K=(-1,0)\cup(0,1)$, which is noncompact, and let its dimensionless coordinate be $x$. Assign entropy per mole
$$
s(x)=s_0-a|x|,\qquad a>0,
$$
where $s_0>a>0$ have units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$. Consider all Borel probability mixtures on $K$ with fixed barycenter $\bar x=0$ and declare them feasible with entropy $\int_Ks\,dP$. This is a constructed mixture model, not a claim that a particular material has this phase domain.
cex-td-noncompact-phase-mixture-no-attai.proof:
1.1 Since $0< s_0-a\le s(x)\le s_0$, every feasible $s$ is nonnegative and bounded. For $n\ge2$, put $A_n:=\{x\in K:|x|\ge1/n\}$. Their union is $K$; since $P(K)=1$, countable additivity implies $P(A_n)>0$ for some $n$. On $A_n$, $s\le s_0-a/n$, and on its complement $s\le s_0$. For any nonnegative simple function $\varphi\le s$, the measure integral definition [F2] therefore gives
$$
\int_K\varphi\,dP\le (s_0-a/n)P(A_n)+s_0P(K\setminus A_n)=s_0-aP(A_n)/n<s_0.
$$
Indeed, refine the finitely many level sets of $\varphi$ by $A_n$ and its complement; each simple-function coefficient is bounded by the corresponding pointwise bound on that piece, so the simple-integral formula [F2] gives the inequality. The common strict upper bound is independent of $\varphi$, hence its supremum also satisfies $\int_Ks\,dP<s_0$. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 For each $0<\epsilon<1$, the measure $P_\epsilon=\tfrac12\delta_{-\epsilon}+\tfrac12\delta_{\epsilon}$ is supported on $K$, has mean zero, and satisfies $\int s\,dP_\epsilon=s_0-a\epsilon$. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ shows that the supremum is $s_0$. Step 1.1 shows that no feasible measure attains it. This lies outside the compactness hypothesis in [F1] and exhibits a finite supremum without a maximizing mixture. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

post-td-canonical-protocol-preparation.title: Canonical initial preparation for a finite protocol
post-td-canonical-protocol-preparation.physical_scope: The start of the specified finite-state protocol is modeled as a canonical preparation at one positive reservoir temperature; preparation success and equilibration are not derived.

references.title: C. Jarzynski, Nonequilibrium Equality for Free Energy Differences
references.locator: Complete four-page paper; canonical initial ensemble and finite-time protocol.

references.title: C. Jarzynski, Introduction to Nonequilibrium Statistical Physics, lecture notes, Nonequilibrium Work Relations
references.locator: Complete 21-page lecture PDF; initial equilibrium preparation and work-relation derivations.

post-td-canonical-protocol-preparation.statement: For a protocol of [[def-td-driven-finite-path-model]], fix a bath temperature $T_b>0$ kelvin and set $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T_b)^{-1}$ in joules$^{-1}$, using the exact constant and SI conventions of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. The finite-state clause of the adopted [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] then gives the stage-zero law $\pi_0(i)=e^{-\beta E_0(i)}/Z_0$; adopt that the initial microstate is drawn from this law, so $\mu_0=\pi_0$. Here $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty and $E_0(i)$ is finite, so $0<Z_0<\infty$ as required by that clause. This is a model premise about the preparation distribution. It does not follow from the finite partition-sum definition, does not assert that an arbitrary system equilibrates in finite time, and does not report a measured preparation. The countable-state and measure-integral branches of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] are not used.

post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy.title: Concave macroscopic fundamental entropy
post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy.physical_scope: The adopted entropy representation for the declared nonrelativistic, macroscopic, additive bulk thermodynamic systems; smooth derivative conditions apply only on the named single-phase charts.

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, Chapter 4 of the complete author-hosted lecture notes, §§4.3.1–4.3.4
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, §§2.5–2.6 and §2.9
Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §§II.F and IV.A

post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy.statement:
For each admitted material constitution $c$, the model adopts a finite scalar function

$$S_c:D_c\longrightarrow\mathbb R\ \text{with values measured in }\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}},$$

on the equilibrium state domain $D_c$ of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. This framework treats $S_c$ as primitive constitutive data: its existence and form are assumed, not derived from the word entropy, statistical mechanics, or experimental evidence.

On every specified convex region $C\subseteq D_c$ in the dimensionless coordinates of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], $S_c$ is continuous and concave, meaning that for all $x,y\in C$ and every $\alpha\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]),

$$S_c((1-\alpha)x+\alpha y)\ge (1-\alpha)S_c(x)+\alpha S_c(y).$$

The domain assumptions are local to the material and region named; no unlisted coordinate tuple is presumed physically realizable. The input of $S_c$ is the represented state $\pi_c(e)$; when the function is written using physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, those coordinates mean the SI values whose dimensionless numerical tuple is $\pi_c(e)$. For independent separated macroscopic systems $A,B$ admitted by [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], entropy is additive under that postulate's composition map $\kappa_{AB}$:

$$S_{A\sqcup B}(\kappa_{AB}(x_A,x_B))=S_A(x_A)+S_B(x_B).$$

On each separately designated open, single-phase chart in the physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, assume the numerical representative of $S_c$ is $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: its first and second coordinate partial derivatives exist and are continuous. The partial derivative $S_U$ at fixed $V,n_1,\ldots,n_r$ is the ordinary partial derivative in the $U$ coordinate, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and is assumed finite and strictly positive. The numerical chart input uses $\hat U=U/(1\,\mathrm J)$; consequently $S_U=(1\,\mathrm J)^{-1}\partial S_c/\partial\hat U$ and has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$. The other physical coordinates are similarly represented using the fixed SI units of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. No differentiability, strict concavity, or positive $S_U$ is asserted outside those charts. This item does not itself define a thermometer calibration or claim a temperature law.

For the tagged bulk family with scaling maps $\delta_\lambda$ and domains $B_{c,\lambda}$ from [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], also adopt, for every admitted $\lambda>0$ and $x\in B_{c,\lambda}$,

$$S_{c^{(\lambda)}}(\delta_\lambda x)=\lambda S_c(x).$$

This is a bulk homogeneity assumption for tagged scaled systems, not exact finite-size scaling for every body. Lieb–Yngvason develop a different accessibility-based route in which entropy is represented from additional operational hypotheses; this framework does not claim that their derivation proves the present primitive entropy postulate.

post-td-entropy-maximum.title: Equilibrium as an attained global entropy maximum
post-td-entropy-maximum.physical_scope: Global stable equilibrium of an explicitly specified isolated macroscopic compound under its stated total-coordinate constraints and permitted exchanges; no claim about local maxima or dynamical relaxation is included.

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, Chapter 4 of the complete author-hosted lecture notes, §§4.3.3–4.3.4
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, §2.9
Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §§II.F and IV.A

post-td-entropy-maximum.statement:
Let $\mathcal F$ be the explicitly declared feasible endpoint set of an isolated compound whose constituents are independent separated macroscopic systems, as defined in [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. For this route, adopt the physical criterion that any endpoint tuple the model classifies as a stable equilibrium under these fixed totals, retained partitions, and permitted exchanges satisfies

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^{\mathrm{eq}})=\max_{x\in\mathcal F}S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x),\qquad S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}S_{c_i}(x_i),$$

Here $\max$ means that $x^{\mathrm{eq}}\in\mathcal F$ and $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^{\mathrm{eq}})\ge S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x)$ for every $x\in\mathcal F$, using maximum in the sense of [[def-max-min]]. The finite sum is as in [[def-finite-sum]], and the summands are those of the separated macroscopic constituents under [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. Whenever the stable-equilibrium label is used, attainment is assumed: at least one maximizing endpoint lies in $\mathcal F$. If $\mathcal F$ is empty or the entropy supremum is not attained, this item supplies no equilibrium state.

“Global” refers to every endpoint in this exact $\mathcal F$, not just nearby states, states reachable by a restricted short-time dynamics, or states on a selected branch. A local maximum that is not global, or a long-lived preparation trapped by kinetic barriers, is not declared stable equilibrium by this postulate. No uniqueness or relaxation dynamics is assumed.

post-td-macroscopic-second-law.title: Macroscopic second law for isolated compounds
post-td-macroscopic-second-law.physical_scope: Endpoint entropy changes for admitted macroscopic processes of an isolated compound, including its named auxiliaries; no pointwise entropy function is assigned to nonequilibrium intermediate configurations.

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, Chapter 4 of the complete author-hosted lecture notes, §4.3
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, §§2.5–2.6
Lieb and Yngvason, The Physics and Mathematics of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, §§II.F and IV.A

post-td-macroscopic-second-law.statement:
For every admitted closed process record $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ of an isolated compound, assume its declared outer boundary is isolated throughout, its material constitution is fixed, its center-of-mass kinetic and separately tracked external-field potential energies have zero endpoint change, and both endpoint preparations are equilibrium macrostates. Include every named auxiliary and work device in the compound, and restrict to constituent splits for which [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] supplies the additive total entropy. The adopted macroscopic second law is

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^+)-S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^-)\ge0,$$

where $S_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the sum of the constituent entropies in [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. The process record and the zero-change conditions are those of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. The process may pass through nonequilibrium configurations; this postulate compares endpoint entropies only and assigns no entropy function to those intermediate configurations.

For an admitted reversible operation in the sense of [[def-td-reversible-process]], adopt zero total entropy change. An admitted irreversible adiabatic operation may have a strictly positive entropy increase, but strict increase is not required for every irreversible operation. The postulate does not state monotonicity for an open compound, an externally driven process, a subsystem that exchanges energy with an omitted environment, or every microscopic trajectory.

post-td-nernst-scoped.title: Uniform Nernst heat-theorem postulate on a compact family
post-td-nernst-scoped.physical_scope: A chosen compact family of fixed-constraint equilibrium branches at strictly positive temperatures in the adopted macroscopic thermodynamic framework; no zero-temperature state, absolute entropy normalization, or microscopic identification is supplied.

references.title: David Tong, Statistical Physics, complete Chapter 4 lecture-note PDF, §4.5
Daniel Arovas, Lecture Notes on Thermodynamics and Statistical Mechanics, Chapter 2, §2.6.2

post-td-nernst-scoped.statement:
Fix a material constitution $c$, a positive temperature $T_0$ in kelvins, and a nonempty compact topological parameter space $K$ of declared external-constraint labels. Here compact means that every open cover of $K$ has a finite subcover; the label $a\in K$ holds its listed external constraints fixed while temperature varies. Let $D_{c,+}\subseteq D_c$ be the designated open equilibrium charts on which the finite $C^2$ entropy and positive absolute temperature $T_c=1/S_{c,U}$ are defined, as in [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] and [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. A model-specified family map
$
\phi:(0,T_0)\times K\longrightarrow D_{c,+}
$
assigns an equilibrium state $\phi(t,a)$ at temperature $t$, so $T_c(\phi(t,a))=t$. The map need not be continuous in $a$; the postulate below itself requires the displayed supremum to be finite for all sufficiently small $t$. Define $S_K(t,a):=S_c(\phi(t,a))$, measured in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$.

The model adopts the following uniform compact-family Nernst heat-theorem postulate:
$
\lim_{t\downarrow0}\ \sup_{a,b\in K}\left|S_K(t,a)-S_K(t,b)\right|=0,
$
where the supremum is the least upper bound of the displayed real differences. This is an additional low-temperature physical postulate, not a consequence of the first or second law. It is a deliberately scoped uniform formulation; it is not asserted equivalent to every statement called the third law or Nernst's theorem.

The postulate constrains entropy differences within the declared family. It does not assert that any individual finite limit $S_K(0,a):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}S_K(t,a)$ exists, that such a limit is zero, or that the family includes every material or constraint. If the indicated individual limit is to be used, its existence and finiteness are an additional premise.

pthm-td-finite-crooks.title: Crooks path and work-distribution relation for a finite protocol
pthm-td-finite-crooks.physical_scope: A path-reversal identity for a finite-state protocol whose stage kernels are reversible with respect to their positive canonical laws; it does not extend to arbitrary driven systems without matching support and reversal assumptions.

references.title: C. Crooks, Entropy production fluctuation theorem and the nonequilibrium work relation for free energy differences
references.locator: Complete six-page paper; microscopic reversibility and canonical endpoint work relation.

references.title: U. Seifert, Stochastic thermodynamics, fluctuation theorems, and molecular machines
references.locator: Sections 3.2.3 and 4.4.1 on forward/reverse work distributions and reversed dynamics.

references.title: C. Jarzynski, Introduction to Nonequilibrium Statistical Physics, lecture notes, Nonequilibrium Work Relations
references.locator: Complete 21-page lecture PDF; comparison of forward and reverse work densities.

pthm-td-finite-crooks.statement: Assume the setup of [[def-td-driven-finite-path-model]], the canonical initial law of [[post-td-canonical-protocol-preparation]], the stationarity model of [[post-td-stationary-bath-kernel]], and, additionally, $\pi_k(i)K_k(i,j)=\pi_k(j)K_k(j,i)$ for every $k,i,j$. For every forward path with positive probability, define its reverse probability by $P_R(\omega^R)=\pi_m(i_m)\prod_{k=1}^mK_k(i_k,i_{k-1})$. Then $P_R(\omega^R)>0$ and $P_F(\omega)/P_R(\omega^R)=e^{\beta(W(\omega)-\Delta F)}$. Consequently, at each work value $w$, $P_F(W=w)=e^{\beta(w-\Delta F)}P_R(W_R=-w)$. The reverse protocol first applies the stage-$k$ reverse transition at fixed $E_k$, then reverses the quench $E_k\to E_{k-1}$; its work is $W_R(\omega^R)=-W(\omega)$.
pthm-td-finite-crooks.proof:
**Given:** [F1], [F2], [A1], [A2], and [F3].

1.1 Define the reverse path law by starting with $\pi_m(i_m)$ and, in reverse order, using $K_k(i_k,i_{k-1})$ at fixed energy $E_k$ before undoing that quench. By detailed balance, if $K_k(i_{k-1},i_k)>0$ then $K_k(i_k,i_{k-1})>0$, because $\pi_k$ is strictly positive. Thus positive forward paths pair with positive reverse paths. [F1, F2, A1, A2]

2.1 On a paired path, divide the endpoint Gibbs weights and use detailed balance for each transition: $P_F(\omega)/P_R(\omega^R)=[\pi_0(i_0)/\pi_m(i_m)]\prod_{k=1}^m[\pi_k(i_k)/\pi_k(i_{k-1})]$. Substituting $\pi_k(i)=e^{-\beta E_k(i)}/Z_k$ and collecting terms gives $\log(P_F/P_R)=\beta[E_m(i_m)-E_0(i_0)-Q_{\mathrm{in}}]+\log(Z_m/Z_0)=\beta(W-\Delta F)$ by [F3]. [F1, F2, F3, A1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The reversed quench at stage $k$ occurs at state $i_{k-1}$, so its work term is $E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})-E_k(i_{k-1})=-[E_k(i_{k-1})-E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})]$; summing proves $W_R(\omega^R)=-W(\omega)$. Summing the path ratio over the finite set of paths with $W=w$ proves the stated distribution identity. [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
